items.name: Gender Studies -- CONTROL r0
items.response:
Empirical work on this question begins by partitioning the observed differential. The Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition splits a raw wage gap into an explained part, attributable to measured characteristics such as schooling, occupation and hours, and an unexplained part. The procedure was first published in 1994. Even though that partition is arithmetically clean, the share it leaves unexplained is not self-interpreting; and whereas the decomposition can work only with the covariates a survey happens to record, a second strategy compares colleagues inside a single establishment. The unexplained residual of a wage decomposition can reflect unmeasured worker characteristics. Comparisons of workers in the same job title at the same firm isolate pay differences attributable to employer decisions.

The within-firm design finds its sharpest application in pay-equity litigation, where the two candidate explanations meet head on. The claimants argued that the pay differential reflected employer discrimination. The employer argued that the pay differential reflected differences in accumulated job tenure. The statutory backdrop frames such disputes: the Equal Pay Act prohibiting sex-based wage differentials was enacted in the United States in 1972, and the rival accounts just rehearsed were pressed only afterwards, once that prohibition was already in force.

Isolating the parenthood channel calls for a different design, one that follows the same workers before and after a first birth rather than comparing different people at a single moment. Kleven, Landais, and Søgaard estimated child penalties using Danish administrative registry data, and those registers show that the long-run earnings penalty for Danish mothers runs at roughly 20 percent. Goldin attributes much of the residual pay gap to "greedy jobs" that reward long and unpredictable hours.

The adjustments behind such a shortfall are observable in administrative panels. Mothers reduce their weekly working hours after the birth of a first child, and it is this retrenchment of hours that produces the long-run earnings penalty of roughly 20 percent recorded for Danish mothers. Because occupations that reward long and unpredictable hours price availability so dearly, mothers also move to employers offering lower wage premiums after the birth of a first child. At least one of these two adjustments, and perhaps both, is at work in any market where the differential widens abruptly at parenthood.

The standing of this literature is reflected in its honours. Either Claudia Goldin was the sole recipient of the 2023 prize in economic sciences, or that prize was shared with at least one other laureate: one of those must be the case, and they cannot both be. For the analyst, the practical upshot is that neither the decomposition, nor the firm-level comparison, nor the event study settles the question alone; attribution rests on whether the gap survives when hours, tenure and employer are held fixed, and on whether it opens at the moment of first birth.
